question: What is the meaning of smart contracts in relation to official declarations (agency or contractor provided, mostly during the life cycle)?
data_group: official declarations (agency or contractor provided, mostly during the life cycle)
description: Smart contracts in relation to official declarations during the product life cycle refer to the automated agreements that ensure the verification of user identities and authorization to perform specific actions as defined in the contract. These smart contracts play a crucial role in validating the identity of service providers, such as repairers and maintenance professionals, during the product use phase. By verifying the identity and permissions of these third-party service providers, smart contracts help maintain data integrity and security throughout the product's life cycle.

As each user in the blockchain keeps a full copy of records that
cannot be deleted, the expanding volume of data collected throughout
the product life cycle can lead to scalability challenges regarding storage
and transaction throughput. The separation of data into on-chain and
off-chain storage is a mechanism proposed for efficient data storage and
scalability of blockchain (Lin et al., 2019). With this approach, only key
data (e.g., core DPP information and properties) are stored on the
blockchain, while other big data are stored on local servers. For instance,
assembly/disassembly instructions and other documentation will be
stored on an off-chain database, while reference pointers to the assem-
bly/disassembly instructions documents are stored on-chain. The on-
chain/off-chain data sync component in this framework ensures data
consistency and facilitates the retrieval of needed information.

3.3.2. Scenario to illustrate the process of enabling information update by a
3rd party service provider during product use phase
This framework can help to enhance data completeness by enabling
3rd party services such as repairers and maintenance professionals to
update the information during the use phase. This is a requirement from
ESPR which is missing in all the current DPP designs. Updating the
service log during the use phase is not included in current DPPs, yet this
is important for consumers because maintenance or repair service
changes may often change the quality and components of the product.
To illustrate the application of our proposed framework, a scenario is
outlined here. Fig. 9 describes the step-by-step workflow of user verifi-
cation for data updates in the service log. The user (a service provider)
can scan the QR code of the EV battery using a product tag scanning App
to get access to the relevant product data in the battery DPP as shown in
steps 1 and 2. The user can choose to view the relevant technical data or
update it as shown in step 3.
To view or update information, the service provider (e.g., repairers,
maintenance professionals) need to prove that they are who they claim
to be (i.e., verification of their identity) and are authorised to perform
the action defined in the DPP access rights and permissions (i.e., what
data the service providers is allowed to access and update). The user’s
identity is then verified using local standard mechanisms such as Cer-
tificate Authorities (CAs) and Membership Service Provider (MSP). An
MSP can be an authorised local identity registry to verify the service
provider. For example, in Norway, the organisation number of a com-
pany/organisation can be looked up and verified using the official reg-
istry (e.g. The Brønnøysund Register Centre). For this case, in Step 4 of
Fig. 9, the service provider provides their 9-digit organisation number
and their email as shown on the left screen in Fig. 10 (left). A smart
contract has a list of authorised service providers for the product. In step
5, a smart contract will verify the user ID with the official registry to
ensure that the organisation is registered and is a legal entity for the
intended role. Afterwards, the smart contract will authenticate the user
using the user organisation’s authentication services and the provided
user credentials. Once verified, the service provider can update the
maintenance information in Step 6, as shown in Fig. 6 (right).
3.3.3. Theoretical implication
Digital solution components, such as the use of blockchain technol-
ogy with smart contracts to verify user identities and control access
rights, have significantly enhanced security at the digital layer. How-
ever, challenges remain in addressing security concerns related to the
transition from physical to digital realms, including risks associated
physical tampering (Jiang et al., 2022). As data carriers serve as the
initial point of access for customers, security measures for this first line
of defence must also be considered. QR codes, commonly used in
